# Introduction: reproducibility as a computational problem {#sec-intro}

*An article about computational science in a scientific
publication is not the scholarship itself, it is merely
advertising of the scholarship. The actual scholarship is
the complete software development environment and the
complete set of instructions which generated the figures.*

[Buckheit and Donoho]{.smallcaps}, paraphrasing Jon
Claerbout, *WaveLab and Reproducible Research* (1995)

## A result that ran only once

Every quantitative health scientist has met the failure
this book exists to prevent. An analysis runs cleanly on
the machine where it was written and produces a table, a
figure, a p-value. A year later, on a new laptop, or a
colleague's, or a reviewer's, the same code errors. Worse,
it may run to completion and return a different number.
The statistics were sound. What failed was everything
around the statistics: a package that changed beneath the
code, a default that shifted between releases of R, a
system library present on one machine and absent on
another. The result had been reproducible exactly once, on
one machine, at one moment, and no one noticed until the
moment had passed.

This book is about closing that gap. Its subject is
computational reproducibility, by which we mean the
property that a computational result can be regenerated,
within a stated tolerance, by another person on another
machine at a later time. That is a narrower claim
than scientific replication, and we shall be careful to
keep the two apart throughout. It is nonetheless a claim
that a great deal of published health-sciences research
cannot currently support. Unlike replication, it is also a
claim that can be secured by technical means available
today.

We begin by fixing the vocabulary of the field and then
review the evidence that computational reproducibility is
often not achieved. We then consider why the failures are
computational in character, and introduce the tools and
the framework that the book uses. Lastly, we set out the
plan of the book and how it is meant to be used.

## What reproducibility means

The vocabulary of this field is contested, and the reader
should fix the terms before wading into the literature. We
follow the distinction adopted by the National Academies
in their 2019 consensus report [@nas2019].
*Reproducibility* is obtaining consistent computational
results using the same input data, computational steps,
methods, code, and conditions of analysis. That is, it is
a statement about re-execution. *Replicability* is
obtaining consistent results across studies aimed at
answering the same question, each with its own data. It is
a statement about whether a scientific finding holds on new
data.
The two are independent. A result can be perfectly
reproducible and entirely wrong, if the code faithfully
regenerates a mistaken number every time. Conversely, a
finding can replicate across laboratories while no single
analysis in the set is computationally reproducible. Leek
and Peng press the point that a reproducible analysis can
still be wrong, and that reproducibility is therefore a
floor rather than a ceiling [@leek2015]. This book
concerns itself almost entirely with the first of the two
terms, and we say so plainly wherever the boundary is in
doubt.

Reproducibility so defined is a spectrum. @peng2011 arranged
computational work along a scale from the merely
published, through code available, code and data
available, and linked and executable, to fully
replicable. He argued that 'reproducibility has the
potential to serve as a minimum standard for judging
scientific claims when full independent replication of a
study is not possible'. We take from Peng
the idea that reproducibility comes in degrees, and that
honesty about which degree one has reached is itself a
scientific virtue. We shall develop that idea into the
levels ladder of @sec-levels.

## The evidence that it is not happening

The case for taking this seriously is empirical, and it is
grim. In psychology, the Open Science Collaboration could
replicate only 39 of 100 studies it re-ran
[@opensciencecollaboration2015]. In preclinical oncology,
@begley2012 reproduced only 6 of 53 landmark findings.
These are replication failures, at the scientific end of
the spectrum, and their causes are many. However, a
growing body of evidence isolates the specifically
computational failures. These are, if anything, more
damning, because they are more avoidable.

@trisovic2022 re-ran more than nine thousand R files
deposited in the Harvard Dataverse. They found that
roughly one in four executed without error, and that was
before asking whether the output matched. @saju2025,
examining R code supplements on the Open Science
Framework, found that only about a quarter ran to
completion. They also found that the vast majority carried
no description of their dependencies at all. These
analyses could not be made to run a second time, so the
question of whether they reached the right conclusion
never arose. The scholarship, in Buckheit and Donoho's
paraphrase of Claerbout, was advertised but never
delivered.

Setting the four studies beside one another, as in
@fig-failure-rates, makes the shape of the problem visible.
The replication studies and the re-execution studies
measure different things, and for that reason the figure
keeps them in separate panels. Nevertheless, the rates are
comparably low in both. The right-hand panel differs in
one respect: it counts failures that better engineering
would fix and that no amount of additional data collection
would.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)

studies <- tibble(
  study = c('Open Science\nCollaboration (2015)',
            'Begley and\nEllis (2012)',
            'Trisovic et al.\n(2022)',
            'Saju et al.\n(2025)'),
  rate = c(39, 11, 26, 25),
  kind = factor(
    c('Replication: new data collected',
      'Replication: new data collected',
      'Re-execution: deposited code re-run',
      'Re-execution: deposited code re-run'),
    levels = c('Replication: new data collected',
               'Re-execution: deposited code re-run')
  )
)

ggplot(studies, aes(x = reorder(study, rate), y = rate)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = kind), width = 0.62, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(rate, '%')),
            hjust = -0.18, size = 3.4) +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, 48)) +
  facet_wrap(~kind, scales = 'free_y', ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    'Replication: new data collected' = '#4c72b0',
    'Re-execution: deposited code re-run' = '#14746f'
  )) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = 'Reported success rate (percent)') +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = 'bold', size = 8.5)
  )
```

The figure tells us how often replication and re-execution
fail. It does not tell us why, and that question is taken
up next.

## Why the failures are computational, not statistical

The reasons re-execution fails point directly at the
remedy. Consider two changes to R itself, each silent and
each capable of altering a published result. In R 3.6.0
the default algorithm that `sample()` uses to turn a seed
into draws changed. Code that set a seed and drew a sample
therefore obtained different draws before and after the
release, with no error and no warning. In R 4.0.0 the
`stringsAsFactors` default flipped from `TRUE` to `FALSE`.
Code reading a data frame then silently produced character
columns where it once produced factors. Any code that
depended on factor-specific behavior, such as the ordering
of levels or a function that requires a factor, behaved
differently as a result. Neither
change was a bug; both were improvements. Both would
nonetheless break the exact reproduction of an analysis
written under the old default, and neither would announce
itself.

These are instances of a general phenomenon. A
computational result depends not only on the code and the
data but on a stack of determinants beneath them. The
stack includes the operating system and its system
libraries, the numerical libraries that implement linear
algebra, the language runtime, the exact versions of every
package, and the session configuration. That
configuration includes the random-number kind, the
contrasts, the number of printed digits, and the locale
and time zone. Underneath all of it sits the hardware. A
published script pins almost none of these. It records the
analysis logic and, if the reader is fortunate, the data.
The remaining layers are left to whatever the next machine
happens to provide. Reproducibility fails in the gap
between what the script fixes and what the result depends
on, and the task of a reproducibility toolchain is to
close that gap, layer by layer. But how far down the stack
has a given effort actually reached? That is the
organizing question of this book.

## The tools, and the framework this book uses

The R ecosystem has, over two decades, produced mature
tools for nearly every layer of that stack. Literate
programming, through `knitr`, R Markdown, and now Quarto
[@allaire2024], binds prose to the code that produces it.
`renv` [@ushey2020] pins package versions in a lockfile.
Docker, through Rocker's R-specific base images
[@boettiger2015; @nust2020rockerverse], pins the operating
system and its libraries. Continuous integration re-runs
the whole compendium on a clean machine to confirm that the
pinned layers actually suffice. Alternatives exist at every
layer: Nix and its R front-end `rix` in place of `renv`
[@dolstra2004; @rodrigues2024rix], Podman or Apptainer in
place of Docker [@kurtzer2017], GitLab in place of GitHub.
We introduce each tool where the chapter ahead needs it,
not in one early catalog. Package pinning appears in
@sec-dependencies, and the environment and its
alternatives in @sec-containers and @sec-backends.
@sec-compendium treats the compendium structure that
@gentleman2007 and @marwick2018's `rrtools` established.
Finally, @sec-pipelines, @sec-testing, and
@sec-verification treat the workflow, quality, and
validation layer.

The difficulty lies in composing this tooling by hand.
`renv` says nothing about the operating system, and Docker
says nothing about which package versions are installed
inside it. Neither says anything about session
configuration. A researcher who wants a genuinely
reproducible analysis must therefore assemble all of it
correctly, for every project, by hand. The running example
of this book uses `zzcollab`, a framework that assembles
the triad (`renv` for packages, Docker for the
environment, continuous integration for validation) into
one workflow. A biostatistician thereby obtains the
composition without building it from scratch. Each chapter
ahead develops the part of `zzcollab` relevant to its own
layer, against the concept it has just introduced.

Like every tool this book covers, `zzcollab` is held to the
standard it teaches. By its own accounting it firmly pins a
part of the [determinant stack](glossary.qmd#gloss-determinant-stack),
namely the environment, the packages, the source, and the
locale and time zone. It leaves the rest (the numerical
libraries, the random-number discipline, the graphics
device, intrinsic non-determinism) to the base image or to
convention. Reproducibility tooling in general has an
adoption problem more than a capability problem.
@saju2025 found that most deposited code supplements
carry no dependency description at all, even though
mature, free, documented tools for that exact
problem have existed for years. The task of this book is
therefore to make existing capability teachable and
routine. It is also to state plainly, at each level of the
ladder, what a given effort has secured and what remains
exposed, including its own.

## The plan of this book

The book is organized in four parts, and three ideas recur
in every chapter. The first is the ladder of
reproducibility levels (L0 locatable, L1 pinned packages,
L2 pinned environment, L3 verified), which we introduce in
@sec-levels and use thereafter as the common scale. The
second is the distinction between capturing
reproducibility and validating it. That is, pinning is
capture, while continuous integration and verification are
validation. The third is the research compendium as the
unit of reproducible work, introduced in @sec-compendium.
The book is written for a one-quarter, ten-week course.
Not every chapter fits in ten weeks, and an instructor
teaching on that schedule should expect to treat some
material as optional. The four parts proceed as follows.

- **Part I, Foundations.** The reproducibility crisis and
  its computational character (@sec-crisis); the levels of
  reproducibility and the determinants that set them
  (@sec-levels); version control with git as the foundation
  of a locatable analysis (@sec-version-control); and the
  research compendium (@sec-compendium).
- **Part II, Capturing the environment.** Pinning packages
  with a lockfile (@sec-dependencies); pinning the operating
  system and runtime with a container (@sec-containers); and
  the alternatives, from Nix to Podman to Apptainer
  (@sec-backends).
- **Part III, Validation.** The practices that let a pinned
  analysis be re-run and checked: literate programming and
  the rendered report (@sec-literate); automating the
  analysis with make and targets (@sec-pipelines); testing and code
  quality (@sec-testing); and continuous integration and
  verification (@sec-verification).
- **Part IV, Collaboration and stewardship.** Sharing a
  compendium with a team and with the world (@sec-archiving).

## How to use this book

The book is meant to be worked, not only read. Each chapter
develops a concept and then builds it, in R and at the
shell, inside a running example compendium. The reader who
follows along will finish with a reproducible project of
their own. More durably, the reader will acquire the
judgment to reason about reproducibility with any
toolchain, and to state without flinching the level a
given analysis has actually reached.

Seven habits recur across the chapters that follow. A
chapter's own rules of thumb will cite a habit by number
rather than restate it. The closing chapter recalls them
once the argument of the book is complete.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Seven habits, and a motto

*Claim only the level you have verified.*

1. Commit before you compute.
2. Pin what you ran, not what is current.
3. Never commit, deposit, or paste restricted data.
4. Make every gate able to fail, and watch it fail once.
5. Compare against a recorded baseline, with a stated tolerance.
6. Rebuild from clean, on a machine that is not yours.
7. Write the honest level down.
:::
